section_1.title: The Hook: Speed vs. Distance
section_1.content: Begin with a visual animation of a 'Robot Runner'. Explain the two directions: calculating instantaneous speed from a position graph (derivative) versus accumulating total distance from a speed graph (integral). This sets the stage for the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
section_1.example: A robot accelerates; the speedometer shows the instantaneous slope (derivative), while the area under the speedometer graph displays the total meters covered (integral).

section_2.title: Review of Prerequisite: The Derivative as a 'Zoom'
section_2.content: Briefly revisit the derivative as the rate of change or the slope of the tangent line. Use a visual 'Zoom-in' effect on a curve to show how we approximate a tiny change (dy/dx).
section_2.example: Zooming into a complex roller-coaster path until it looks like a straight line to find the slope at one specific second.

section_3.title: The Integral as 'Summation'
section_3.content: Transition to the integral. Visualize it as slicing an area into infinite, paper-thin rectangles (Riemann sums). Explain that adding these up gives the total accumulation.
section_3.example: Filling a tank with water: The rate of water flow (speed) is the derivative, and the total volume of water in the tank over time is the integral.

section_4.title: The Fundamental Bridge
section_4.content: Reveal the core concept: Differentiation and Integration are inverse operations, much like addition and subtraction. Show a 'Cycle Animation' where a function F(x) is differentiated to f(x), and f(x) is integrated back to F(x).
section_4.example: If a squirrel collects acorns at a rate of f(t), the total pile size is the integral of that rate. If you want to know the rate of collection at any moment, take the derivative of the total pile size.

section_5.title: Summary & Application
section_5.content: Conclude by emphasizing that the 'Integral' recovers the 'Anti-derivative'. This connection allows us to solve complex physical problems by simply finding the inverse process.
section_5.example: A SpaceX rocket launch: Using the rate of fuel burn (derivative) to predict the exact moment the rocket reaches a specific altitude (integral).
